extracted.intended_audience: aspiring cartoonists and humorists (especially single-panel/New Yorker/Instagram cartoonists)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative criteria for creating single-panel (gag) cartoons — both slow-crafted magazine-style pieces and quick social-media cartoons — emphasizing setup, punch, voice, and strategies to make a cartoon 'land.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific, awkward sense of humor
rubrics_metrics.description: A distinct personal voice that is specific and awkward; a recognizable comic sensibility that builds a cult following.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate a narrowly specific tone rather than generic jokes — the awkwardness and specificity of perspective is a feature that attracts a devoted audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poke at contradictions and absurdities of daily life/parenting
rubrics_metrics.description: Focus on the contradictions and absurdities found in everyday life and modern parenting as fodder for jokes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mine small, real social tensions and parental frustrations and exaggerate or invert them into comic situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dry, philosophical reflections
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a dry voice and occasionally philosophical or reflective angles to give the cartoon emotional or intellectual heft.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance punchlines with small philosophical observations to deepen resonance rather than relying only on surface gags.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thematic attention (class, equality, access)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recurring themes can include social topics such as class, equality, and access, which inform subject choices and subtext.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let these themes shape the situations you depict — the cartoon can be funny while signaling a consistent moral or topical interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Setup: recognizable everyday moment
rubrics_metrics.description: Setup: present something most readers will recognize — an ordinary situation or small social moment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use everyday specificity so readers immediately identify with the scene; the setup should be familiar enough that the punch subverts expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punchline: subversion via visual or caption
rubrics_metrics.description: Punchline: the visual element or caption that upends the setup, creating the joke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The punch can be delivered visually, textually, or (ideally) by the interaction of both; it should refract the setup into something unexpected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual + caption compression
rubrics_metrics.description: The drawing and caption together must carry compressed meaning; the combination should convey more than either element alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for economy: every line and word should contribute to the joke. Compression increases recognition and impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawing imperfection as authenticity signal
rubrics_metrics.description: Imperfect, human drawing quality often signals authenticity and can make jokes land better than polished art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't over-sterilize the line work; visible imperfections can make the voice feel immediate and relatable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specificity of small social moment
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose very specific small social moments (micro-situations) as the basis for the gag.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detail anchors the joke — the more particular the moment, the more likely a viewer can think 'that's me' and feel recognized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition ('I've felt that')
rubrics_metrics.description: A successful cartoon evokes the response 'I've felt that' — it should create empathy through recognition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test whether the idea triggers personal recognition; if readers can map it to their own experience, it will land more strongly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punch type: single (haiku) vs compound (sonnet)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish between single concise punches (Instagram-style 'haiku') and compound, layered jokes (New Yorker-style 'sonnet').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide which form suits the idea: quick, single-note revelations work for social posts; multi-layered irony or buildup suits slower, magazine pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: New Yorker Cartoons (Sonnets) — slow-cooked process
rubrics_metrics.description: A mode of production characterized by slow thinking and disciplined practice: spend time thinking (e.g., a day per week), cultivate calm, and practice 'scales.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat magazine-style work as craft: step back, iterate, and polish. Work benefits from extended rumination and disciplined exercises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instagram Cartoons (Haikus) — immediate single-take process
rubrics_metrics.description: A fast-production mode: one-take drawings photographed and posted within minutes; often one clear punch and serves as personal processing of annoyances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use immediacy to capture raw reactions; these pieces can be looser and more spontaneous, with the punch often coming directly from a current irritation or observation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought bubble made literal (modern strategy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Make internal thoughts visually manifest — literalizing the thought bubble as a device for humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this tactic to externalize private internal monologue in visually surprising ways.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal monologue externalized (modern strategy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Turn private mental commentary into visible dialogue or imagery to create comedic contrast with the scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The humor often comes from the mismatch between outward behavior and inner commentary; exaggerate that tension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parenthood scenes magnified to absurdity (modern strategy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Exaggerate ordinary parenting situations into absurd extremes to reveal the emotional truth and comic potential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amplify small parental frustrations into surreal or hyperbolic visuals that reveal recognizable emotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anxiety personified (modern strategy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Represent anxiety as a character or visible force in the cartoon to literalize an internal state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personifying anxiety can make abstract feelings concrete and funny; use visual metaphor to convey psychological truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finck-style checklist: Is there a recognizable everyday setup?
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicit checklist item from Finck's rubric asking whether the cartoon begins with an everyday setup recognizably familiar to readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the setup is too obscure, the punch may not register; prioritize universal-seeming moments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finck-style checklist: Does the visual + caption combine to make the punch?
rubrics_metrics.description: Checklist item asking whether both image and text work together to produce the joke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate synergy: neither element should be redundant; ideally the joke emerges only when both are read together.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finck-style checklist: Is the punch single (haiku) or compound (sonnet)?
rubrics_metrics.description: Checklist item prompting identification of punch complexity to determine appropriate form and pacing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match execution to punch complexity: avoid over-elaborating a single-note punch or under-developing a compound idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finck-style checklist: Does it process a real anxiety/contradiction?
rubrics_metrics.description: Checklist item asking whether the cartoon is working through an authentic anxiety or social contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humor grounded in real emotional or social contradictions tends to resonate more deeply than purely gimmicky jokes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finck-style checklist: Could a viewer say 'that's so me'?
rubrics_metrics.description: Checklist item measuring whether the reader can personally relate to the cartoon's situation or feeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for identifiability; if readers can insert themselves into the moment, the cartoon achieves recognition and impact.
